doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Waiting for the song to talk: Jungleland and Roberto Carlos
summary: Prompted by Ray Conniff, he describes waiting for the song, writing the strings on Jungleland, and writing to evoke feeling, as with Roberto Carlos.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You know who said something very similar was Ray Conniff.

He was writing for big bands and he was very happy doing it but he was writing for the guys he said. And then he got interested, the band leader got interested, he said, “Write some bop for us.” He said, “Naa I don’t want to.” And then he was out of work. And he thought you know I’ve been writing for the musicians, what if I wrote for the people who are buying the records. And I’m so happy to hear you say that. And I don't know if you recall but we had a phone conversation about a year ago and I saved my notes. And you said, “I wait for the song to talk to me.”

Ah, yes. And you know this is the fiftieth anniversary of Bruce Springsteen’s “Born to Run” album. And I wrote the strings on “Jungleland.” And the first time I really realized that I had to wait for the song to talk to me was when I wrote that arrangement. Normally I could write an arrangement for strings, a couple hours. So I went down to my office in New Jersey, to my basement. And I said I’ve got to write two arrangements for the session tomorrow. I started at 11 o’clock and I figured I’d be writing until two in the morning, I’d knock them off. It took me six hours to write that arrangement because I finally listened to the song. And I finally listened to where the record was going. And I met with Bruce. And Bruce knew he wanted strings on the record but really couldn’t identify exactly what he wanted. In fact in the meeting he just, after ten minutes he says, “No, you do it.” He says, “I’ll see you tomorrow.” But what was really interesting about it is eventually I started to hear what I needed to put on the record. And it sort of changed the way I approached writing string arrangements. But that was a process that was coming because I had made several arrangements that I remembered I just had to sit there and wait for it to come.
Was it partly the lyric content that led you in the direction?
I can’t really say that it was any one thing. For many years I recorded Roberto Carlos, who is from Brazil. And I understand Portuguese and he would play me his demo on a © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

piano, or on a keyboard, that he had recorded. And I heard him singing in Portuguese but he would tell me what it meant in English. And as he would tell me the story I could get the feeling of what he was saying. And the interesting part about – I learned about making records is when you listen to a record you may not remember what the lyric says. You may not remember what the melody was all at one time. But you’ll really remember how it made you feel. So the whole idea was to get you to feel exactly what I felt making the arrangement. And if I could sit there and get chills when I was writing and say, “Oh I can’t wait to hear this,” I knew my enthusiasm being pored into the paper would eventually evoke a feeling in somebody else because we all feel joy, we all feel love, we all feel all these passions. And well maybe you didn’t get it, but that person will get it, and maybe that person will get the feeling but there’ll be two other people here that didn’t get it. And that was a process of going through and learning that if it killed me when I was writing it, then I could just say, “Well what have you been doing, Charlie?” Say, “Hey check this out.” And I knew that, because they were on the same plane, if they heard it they would get the same feeling.
